title: Network lab 1: Your first network (Filius)
summary: Install Filius, cable four computers to a switch, give them addresses, and prove with ping which ones can talk and why one can't.

script.intro: Welcome to your first network lab. Banyan Books is a small bookshop, and today you're setting up its front office: two tills, an office computer, and one more that someone has typed in wrongly. We'll do it in Filius, a free network simulator made for school lessons. By the end you'll have cabled four computers to a switch, used ping to prove which ones can talk, and read the packets that explain why one of them can't. Keep README.txt open beside you: it has the addressing plan.
script.outro: Three ideas to keep from today. A netmask decides which addresses are local. A computer only talks directly to addresses in its own network, however good the cabling is. And before the first packet, ARP finds the hardware address to send it to. See you in lab two.

steps.say: Step one: install Filius and meet its two modes. Download it from lernsoftware-filius.de. On Windows the installer is easiest; on a Mac or on Linux, the zip runs anywhere Java is installed. Start it and choose English. Now look at the toolbar. Filius has two modes, and most beginner mistakes come from being in the wrong one.
steps.after: The hammer is design mode. That's where you place devices, draw cables and type settings. The green play arrow is simulation mode. That's where the network actually runs, and you sit at the computers and type commands. You can't change an address while the simulation runs, and you can't ping anything in design mode. Down the left is the parts bin: Computer, Switch, Cable and more. So the mode for placing and cabling devices is design.

steps.say: Step two: cable four computers to a switch. In design mode, drag one switch and four computers onto the canvas. Pick the cable tool, click a computer, then click the switch. Filius picks a free port for you, so there's no counting ports. Do all four. Then click each computer in turn and type its name, IP address and netmask from the plan.
steps.after: Three of them are in 192.168.1, numbered 11, 12 and 13. The fourth, stray, gets 192.168.2.14, and that's on purpose. The netmask on every computer is 255.255.255.0. That mask says the first three numbers name the network and the last number names the computer. So till-1, till-2 and office are all in network 192.168.1, and stray, on the same switch with the same kind of cable, is in network 192.168.2. Keep that in your head; it's about to matter. If the names don't show on the canvas, untick Use IP address as name.

steps.say: Step three: ping, and explain the one that fails. Press the green arrow. Click till-1 and open Software installation. Add Command line, and press Apply. Now open the command line. First type ipconfig, to check the computer agrees with the plan. Then ping till-2 at 192.168.1.12, office at 192.168.1.13, and finally stray at 192.168.2.14.
steps.after: ipconfig shows till-1's own address and netmask, exactly as you typed them. The pings to till-2 and office come back with replies. The ping to stray fails. Nothing is wrong with the cable, and nothing is wrong with the switch. The problem is the address. Before till-1 sends anything, it compares the destination with its own network. 192.168.2.14 isn't in 192.168.1, so till-1 won't try to reach it directly. It would hand the packet to a router, but there is no router, so it gives up. Write that in one line: a different network, and no router to get there. So the answers are no, and ipconfig.

steps.say: Step four: fix it, and watch the data exchange. Go back to design mode, click stray, and change its address to 192.168.1.14. Run the simulation again and ping it from till-1. It answers. Now right-click till-1, choose Show data exchange, ping stray once more, and read the list from the top.
steps.after: Look above the first ping. The first packets aren't ICMP at all, they're ARP. To put a frame on the cable, till-1 needs stray's hardware address, its MAC address, and so far it only knows the IP address. So it asks everyone on the switch at once: who has 192.168.1.14? Every computer hears the question, and only stray answers, with its MAC address. Then come the ICMP echo requests and echo replies, the ping itself. Ping again and there's no new ARP, because till-1 remembers the answer for a while, in what's called the ARP cache. The protocol that finds the MAC address is ARP.

steps.say: That's the end of lab one. You built a network, broke it on purpose, and read the packets that fixed it. Every lab in this set works the same way: the work happens in a free program on your own computer, and you answer the questions on this page as you go. Network lab two adds a router, so two networks can finally talk.
